Albino killings in Malawi

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The UN has declared that people with Albinism in Malawi are at risk of "total extinction" unless radical action is taken to protect them

Summary:
Malawi has an albino population of 10 000, in May this year the UN announced that this population is at risk of extinction due to kidnappings and attacks for their body parts. 18 Albino's haven been killed and 64 attacked over a 2 year period.

Edna Cedrick's 2 year old Albino son was kidnapped in May this year, his twin brother is all she has left. She tells us the story of the day he was taken and how she fears for him every single day.
We have made contact with a man who worked in the black market of Albino body parts. For two arms, two legs and a tongue you can get 75000$, which is way more than the fine or small sentences handed down for alleged Albino body part trading. He is willing to speak, he is out on bail so we will have to hide his identity.
We would also want to speak to the head of the traditional healers association about how these parts are being used in traditional medicine and magic. What is the ideology behind it and why are they condemning those that are still practicing this?

In Tanzania they have lowered these type of killings by registering all Albino's in the country, monitoring them and offering safe houses. In Malawi there is no such protection and it is feared that the increase in attacks in Malawi is because of these tighter regulations in Tanzania. The traders are crossing the borders.
Is this happening in SA?
Not on this scale at all. But, the Albinism society of South Africa is willing to be interviewed and speak about the threat to people living with albinism in South Africa.
We have one case study in SA, but that is all. The biggest problem on the continent at the moment is in Malawi

Edna Cedrick's

Press Release:


Albino Terror
What has led the United Nations to declare that people with albinism—a congenital disorder characterized by the complete or partial absence of pigment in the skin, hair and eyes—are at risk of total extinction, unless radical action is taken to protect them? Carte Blanche meets people living with this disorder and with unimaginable fear, people for whom something as simple as going to school or venturing a little too far from home could see them pay the ultimate price?

Transcript
Albino
TV Cut

Pages
Tarryn Crossman – Director / Producer

Characters:
Edna Cedric

00:00 -00:21 Establishing of Malawi V/O: Long back then and up to now, there is a belief that people with Albinism they don’t die but they disappear. They would actually kill them because it was like an omen to have a child with albinism within the family.
00:21 – 00:42 Graveyard. Edna Cedric, mother with albino child Edna: At first I had two albino children and we were living very happy in peace. The boys were always chatting and playing together all the time. When my sons were born, people in the village were happy and accepted them. But ads they grew older some people started showing negativity towards them.
00:42 – 01:23 Interview with the uncle of attack victim, Dickson Lawasha Mariam is my niece. The daughter to my sister. She is the third born in the family. As a family, we were happy that we had a child; we accepted that the child was born with that condition and overall she was God’s creation and is a human being just like us. Mariam’s parents passed away and after they passed my other sister took her in to take care of her. But soon after her mother passed, on the 5th of January at around 8 o0’clock in the evening thugs came and abducted Mariam.
01:23 – 01:50 V/O In rural Malawi 2015 attacks and murders with people with Albinism dramatically increased. With 18 Albinos being murder and 64-attempted murder and kidnapping taking place in one year. In May 2016 the UN declared that the 10 000strong populations in Malawi are at risk of extinction. If something is not done soon to protect these vulnerable people.
01:50 – 02:13 Action Amos Executive Director of The Federation of Disability Organisation In Malawi The general belief amongst the populous in Malawi is that body parts of persons with albinism do bring luck and charm so any body parts that they can get hold of be the hair, the toes the hands it can assists someone to enhance their luck also to improve businesses.
02:13 - 02:24 Interview with Dave Sulumba spokesperson Machinga Police Station. Dave: They believe that if they have human body that is for an albino they can use it for rituals maybe magic they use it for magic.
02:24 – 03:02 Kandulo Pangaunye – president of the Traditional Healers Association Kandulo: I look after all the traditional healers in Malawi from the southern region up to the northern region. We’ve got a lot of members almost 40000. There’s no medicine that we know that uses the flesh of an albino. This is a new story to me if you think a traditional doctor is doing this it is someone from another country.
03:02 – 03:15 Action: When Tanzania enhanced their security with persons of albinism and out lawed the witch doctors in that country. I think the market there moved to Malawi.
03:15 – 03:24 Dickson: There were rain showers late in the afternoon that day they captured her and she was naked. They made her walk 25km without clothes.
03:24 – 03:51 Interview with Mariam the victim Mariam: We were coming from playing that day. When we arrived home we went to bed to sleep and the next thing I realised that I was outside the house. I screamed and they pulled me into a ditch. I was running and the other people were following me. I was running, running.
03:51 – 03:59 V/O V/O: after trying to escape numerous times Mariam’s abductors bound her hands together and took her by bicycle to her first potential buyer
03:59 – 04:11 Mariam: After that we went to a house with lights we found decapitated heads and I ran outside. They moved me to the other side (of the house).
04:11 – 04:29 Dickson: The abductors started negotiating with the buyers but they didn’t want a child with albinism they wanted a white child. They failed to sell her, so they travelled 25km to Anpiz and started to phone other buyers. And they left her at the house. They untied her and she found a chance to run
04:29 – 04:34 V/O VO: after escaping from her captures Mariam managed to hide till daylight.
04:34 -04:54 Dickson: And when we found her the next morning by the river she was bruised and wounded from being dragged by her abductors. As a family, regardless of this shocking ordeal, we were just thankful to god that she was alive.
04:54 – 05:02 V/O V/O: on the first of January 2016 in a remote village in the south of Malawi this mother’s life was changed forever.
05:02 – 05:35 Edna: I was with my twin sons sleeping in the middle of the night when I woke up to take my one of them to the bathroom. When we went back to sleep a few minutes later the abductors knocked down the door and invaded our house. They tied me up in our mosquito net while they beat my children.
05:35 – 05:40 V/O V/o: Edna tried everything to fight off her attaches but they were too strong.
05:40 – 05:56 Edna: By that time they took my boy outside and I heard a voice from one of them saying, “cut her up”. That’s when they came inside and hacked me with a machete.
05:56 – 6:00 V/O V/O: this would be the last time that Sonto would see her son Harry, alive.
6:00 – 06:15 Edna: Two days later the search crew went to a village called Kalawile and there they only found a decapitated head. The child’s name was Harry Mokoshoni.
06:16 – 06:29 Dave: One of the suspects was the chief within the area and one of them was the uncle to the victim. The suspects are in jail waiting for court proceedings.
06:30 – 07:00 Action: there’s also an element of ignorance amongst the populist. People that are rich are the ones that send poor people or entice them to sell their children. When people have a lot of money and think that they can be quite rich in a short period that again is total ignorance. So really without a proper inquiry it’s very difficult to determine what is fuelling this.
07:00 – 07:12 Kandulo: Traditional healers are too poor because if they take the flesh of an albino it is too expensive for a traditional healer to buy. Traditional healers don’t have any money. Even if you look at his clothes you can see that he is poor
07:12 -07:27 V/O: The general concusses seems to be that these abductions and murders are being orcastrated by people with money. But one way or another these albino body parts need to land up in traditional healers in order for the muthi or charms to be created.
07:27 – 07:46 In the past the maximum sentence of human tissue is a fine of 20000 Kwacha = R35. But as for now the laws have been amended but now the maximum punishment for people involving with albinism is 21 years to life in prison.
07:46 – 08:11 Action: this has been a cultural thing over a period of time changing of behaviour is quote a challenge. So government has to enhance his efforts to sensitize populist through civic education. It’s about educating the masses so that they get to know people with albinism like any other persons not any other difference.
O8: 11 – 08:51 Dickson: she is scared whenever she’s moving around because some of the people who abducted her were released from police custody. One day when Miriam was at school, she was on of the abductors watching her from afar. It was around 10am when during recess. She then ran back to the class and notified the headmaster and the man ran away. Miriam is still scared to move around
08:51 – 08:56 Miriam: Sometimes I’m scared but sometimes I’m not.
08:56 – 09:10 Edna: My remaining son always asks me about his brother and wants to know where he is. He still remembers his brother. I miss my child so much
